name: Torricelli's Law
statement: Fluid escapes a hole at the speed it would reach falling from the surface above it.
statementAccent: the speed it would reach falling
meaning: Torricelli's law gives the speed of fluid draining from an opening in a tank under gravity. That speed equals the speed a body would gain by falling freely through the height of the fluid surface above the hole, so it is the square root of two times gravity times that height. A deeper hole, with more liquid above it, produces a faster jet, and as the tank empties and the level drops, the jet slows.
mechanism: The result follows from conservation of energy: the kinetic energy the escaping fluid carries away matches the potential energy lost as liquid falls from the surface to the level of the hole, which gives the speed as the square root of two times gravity times the height. It is a special case of Bernoulli's principle applied between the free surface and the orifice, both at atmospheric pressure, for an idealised incompressible, inviscid fluid in a tank wide enough that the surface itself barely moves.

examples.text: Water spurting from a hole in the side of a tank leaves at a speed set only by the depth of liquid above the hole, then arcs away as a projectile.
As a container empties, the height above the hole falls, so the jet steadily slows — the discharge is fast at first and tapers off.
Ancient water clocks had to reckon with this falling speed, since a vessel does not drain at a constant rate as its level drops.

variants.name: The discharge coefficient
variants.text: Real orifices deliver less than the ideal flow: the jet narrows just past a sharp-edged hole, the vena contracta, so the actual rate is the ideal times a coefficient around 0.65 for water.

variants.name: A case of Bernoulli
variants.text: Torricelli's law is Bernoulli's principle specialised to a draining tank, recovering the same square-root-of-height speed from energy conservation along a streamline.

whyItMatters: It is the foundational result for efflux — how fast and how much fluid leaves an opening — used in hydraulics, tank and spillway design, and any estimate of draining or leaking. Simple and memorable, it captures the essential physics of gravity-driven outflow, and its idealised form is the baseline that engineering corrections refine.

working.text: use the vertical distance from the free surface down to the orifice, not the total tank height or the size of the hole.
remember the speed falls as the level drops, so draining is not at a constant rate.
multiply the ideal flow by a discharge coefficient to account for the vena contracta and viscosity in practice.

limits: It is an idealisation, a special case of Bernoulli's principle, assuming an inviscid, incompressible fluid, atmospheric pressure on both the surface and the jet, and a tank much wider than the hole so the surface velocity is negligible. Real orifices fall short: the jet contracts past a sharp edge, the vena contracta, so the true flow is the ideal reduced by a discharge coefficient, and viscosity slows the efflux further. The law gives the ideal speed, not directly the real volumetric flow rate, which depends on the effective opening.
misreadings: The height in the formula is the depth of the surface above the hole, not the tank's full height or the size of the opening. The ideal speed depends only on that height and gravity, not on the fluid's density or the hole's area, which instead affect the flow rate and draining time. And the formula gives the ideal efflux speed; the actual discharge is smaller because of the vena contracta and viscosity.
origin: Stated by the Italian physicist Evangelista Torricelli in 1643, in his work on the motion of fluids appended to 'Opera Geometrica' (1644); Torricelli, who also invented the barometer, was an assistant and follower of Galileo in Galileo's final months.
